title: Degradation storyboarding and capacity escape hatch
author: Ava Patel
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the Degradation Storyboarding process and an associated Capacity Escape Hatch runbook for model inference services. It brings together SLO/error-budget thresholds, capacity triggers, telemetry and evidence collection, and step-by-step mitigation actions to contain user-visible degradation while protecting critical tenants.

Scope:
- Applicable services: inference-router, runtime-pool, kv-cache, embedding-worker (model-serving fleet).
- Applicable failures: sustained latency tail growth, progressive error-rate rise, cache blowups, and multi-tenant headroom exhaustion.
- Out of scope: hardware maintenance windows and planned upgrades (handled by maintenance playbooks).

Why this doc exists:
- Engineering teams need a repeatable, low-friction process to storyboard degradation scenarios (what degrades first, who notices, and what fallback actions preserve SLAs).
- SREs need clear, tested escape hatches to drain or throttle traffic with minimal customer impact and precise evidence for post-incident review.

Definitions and key thresholds:
- SLO (p99 latency): 200ms for text-generation endpoints in hosted tier.
- Error budget unit: normalized per-tenant token-weighted burn rate.
- Degradation Alert Levels:
  1) Watch: sustained p99 > 180ms for 3 minutes AND token rate unchanged.
  2) Degraded: p99 > 220ms OR 5% increase in 5m error rate.
  3) Critical: p99 > 400ms OR error rate > 10% OR headroom < 8% cluster-wide.

Telemetry and evidence to collect (minimum):
- Metrics (time-series): inference-router.p99_latency, runtime-pool.cpu_util, runtime-pool.gpu_mem_free, kv-cache.hit_ratio, tenant.token_rate, tenant.error_rate.
- Traces: representative 95/99 traces for degraded requests (include model_id, sequence_len, batching_time).
- Logs: runtime OOM events, kernel-fallback warnings, preemption/eviction events.
- Capacity snapshots: cluster free_gpus, instance types, soft_reserved_capacity per-tenant.

Example telemetry table (copyable):
Metric | Query | Threshold for action
inference-router.p99_latency | sum(rate(inference_router_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le) -> p99 | > 220ms -> Degraded
runtime-pool.gpu_mem_free | avg(gpu_mem_free_bytes) by (zone) | < 12% -> Watch
kv-cache.hit_ratio | avg(kv_cache_hit_ratio) by (model) | < 60% -> Watch
tenant.token_rate | sum(rate(tenant_tokens[1m])) by (tenant) | > forecasted + 25% -> Consider soft-priority

Degradation storyboarding process (how to map cause -> user impact -> mitigation):
1) Identify the initial signal: SRE/alerting or oncall receives a Watch/Degraded alert. Capture the earliest metric and the query that fired.
2) Map scope: determine impacted tenants, regions, models, and queue backlog. Use tenant-scorer to identify top-10 affected tenants by token volume.
3) Create a degradation storyboard: for each affected tenant, document the observed symptom, the likely failure mode (e.g., batching stall, KV cache miss storm), the user-visible effect (e.g., chat latency, truncation), and 3 prioritized mitigations.
4) Apply non-invasive mitigations first (metric-level throttling, increase batching time limit for low-priority routes, promote cached model variants).
5) If non-invasive steps do not stabilize within the cookbook window (15 minutes), escalate to the Capacity Escape Hatch (below).

Capacity Escape Hatch (runbook) — intent: reclaim safe headroom or reduce risk surface while minimizing global impact.
Pre-conditions:
- Degraded or Critical alert state AND verification of sustained telemetry for at least 5 minutes.
- Incident lead (SRE) or oncall engineer assigned.
- Evidence bundle prepared (metrics, sample traces, tenant list).

Escape Hatch checklist (ordered):
1) Soft SLO gating (recommended): enable dynamic admission-control with the following parameters:
   - global_admission.mode = "priority-aware"
   - global_admission.priority_threshold = 0.75 (allows highest-priority tenants first)
   CLI: rdoctl admission enable --mode priority-aware --threshold 0.75
2) Throttle non-critical routes: apply token-weight limit for background embeddings and batch-async endpoints.
   CLI: rdoctl throttle set --route /v1/embeddings --max-qps 1000 --scope tenant:noncritical
3) Redirect model variants: failover traffic from full_fp16 models to quantized-INT8 variants for non-SLA tenants.
   CLI: rdoctl routing apply --from model:openlm-7b-fp16 --to model:openlm-7b-int8 --scope tenant:low-priority
4) Evict soft-reserved capacity: where permissible, reclaim reserved GPU slices from test tenants (eviction must follow eviction-policy-tag).
   CLI: rdoctl capacity reclaim --tag test-evict --grace 30s --notify-team infra-oncall
5) Warm-up standby pools: if cold pools exist, trigger scale-up to standby pool (prefer same-region).
   CLI: rdoctl pools scale --name standby-pool-eu --min 2 --target 8 --reason "escape-hatch"
6) Controlled tenant drain: for tenants still responsible for >40% headroom erosion, perform targeted traffic drain with pre-configured fallback behaviors (retries, reduce tokens-per-request).
   Steps to drain:
     a) Notify customer via automated channel (internal-runbook notification).
     b) Apply per-tenant admission reduction: rdoctl tenant throttle --tenant $TENANT_ID --max-rate 25%
     c) Monitor for stabilization 2m. If no improvement, increase throttle to 50%.

Abort criteria (when to stop escape hatch):
- p99 latency returns below 200ms and headroom > 15% sustained for 10 minutes.
- Error rate normalizes to baseline for 10 minutes.

Rollback criteria (reverse actions safely):
- Re-enable routes in reverse order of application (start with traffic redirects, then admission-control, then capacity reclaim).
- If rollback causes immediate re-degradation, revert last action and document in the incident timeline.

Ownership and escalation:
- Incident lead (SRE): responsible for running the storyboard and executing the escape hatch.
- Infra-oncall: performs capacity reclaim, pool scaling, and VM/instance-level actions.
- Platform-release: approves model-variant routing and global admission changes if any persistent configuration changes are required.
- Escalation path: SRE lead -> SRE manager -> Platform engineering manager -> CTO (for customer-impacting multi-region incidents).

Post-incident evidence and retrospective requirements:
- Attach evidence bundle to the incident: metric snapshots, 5 representative traces per impacted tenant, probe-run outputs, capacity snapshots.
- Incident review template must include:
  1) Timeline with actions and timestamps (UTC).
  2) Root cause hypothesis and verification steps.
  3) Escape hatch actions taken and rationale.
  4) What worked / what did not.
  5) Action items owning a remediation (owner, priority, due date).
- Required follow-ups: a stress-test that reproduces the observed pattern in staging and a runbook revision within 7 days.

Operational tooling and automation suggestions (to reduce manual steps):
- Playbook automation: a gated automation that can run steps 1–3 (admission control, throttle, variant redirect) with a 2-step manual approval.
- Evidence bundler: one-click collection of p99 time-series, top-10 tenant traces, and last-200 runtime logs; stores bundle in incident S3 bucket.
- Storyboard templates: pre-populated Confluence template per-service to capture storyboard items and mitigations.

Periodic exercises and verification:
- Run degradation storyboarding tabletop every quarter with at least two live drills per year that exercise full escape-hatch steps (including eviction and controlled tenant drain).
- Verify automations in a canary cluster monthly.

Appendix: common failure modes and quick mitigations
- KV cache storm: increase cache size for hot-models, enable per-tenant cache quotas, roll back model changes that increased key cardinality.
- Large-sequence surges: apply max_sequence_len guardrails, promote batching time to avoid underfilled batches.
- Batch stall from head-of-line blocking: enable request reordering for background routes.
